recentItems.title: Dozens of Saudi air strikes pound Houthi positions as Yemen fighting rages
recentItems.description:
Yemen's Ansar Allah Houthis say Saudi Arabia has launched a wave of air strikes across five regions — Lahj, Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Hajjah — as Riyadh supports Yemen's internationally recognised government in countering a rapid Houthi offensive. 
The Iran-backed group has advanced west and south in the past week, seizing territory including the Red Sea port of Mocha. 
Injuries have been reported in Taiz. For its part, Saudi Arabia is accusing the Houthis of carrying out deliberate attacks on civilians, saying the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at civilian infrastructure in Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif, injuring 13 people. 
The Houthis released video they say shows a Saudi air strike in Hodeidah province, as well as footage of fighters in Mocha celebrating their advance. 
The Saudi air strikes are forcing the Houthis to redeploy and minimise their visibility, with the group adopting what it calls a “stealth mode” as attacks target their positions across multiple provinces. 
Saudi Arabia is also striking areas such as Hajjah, where no clashes are taking place, because it believes missiles and drones are being launched from there. 
The Houthis have continued targeting Saudi Arabia, particularly Jizan, with Saudi oil assets identified as a main target. 
The Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia are seeking to prevent the Houthis from expanding deeper into government-held territory, while a source says Riyadh is trying to convince the US and other regional powers to join the military effort and halt further advances towards Taiz and Marib. 

Al Jazeera's Yousef Mawry reports from Sanaa.

recentItems.title: Israeli opposition challenges Netanyahu on security but backs continued wars
recentItems.description:
Israel is preparing for parliamentary elections on October 27, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeking another term amid growing opposition over his handling of the country's security and regional wars. Opposition parties are presenting themselves as an alternative on security and foreign policy, but most are not calling for an end to Israel's military campaigns. Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party is leading several recent polls, says Netanyahu failed to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear capability and has called for the removal of Iran's enriched uranium. Yair Lapid has gone further, arguing that Israel and its allies should target Iranian energy infrastructure to put pressure on the country's economy. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett has called for a regional alliance against Iran and what he describes as Islamist and “radical” forces, including Qatar and Turkiye. The opposition and Netanyahu's coalition also share support for maintaining Israel's occupation of southern Lebanon, highlighting how the election debate is focused more on how Israel fights its wars than whether it should continue them. 

Al Jazeera's Nour Odeh reports.

recentItems.title: Nepal floods: Former MP loses 40 family members in Rasuwa disaster
recentItems.description:
Nepal is still assessing the scale of destruction caused by last month's flash floods, which swept away entire towns and villages near the border with China's autonomous region of Tibet. 
At least 1,350 people have been confirmed dead and another 5,000 are missing and presumed buried under the mud. 
In the worst-hit Rasuwa district, former MP Dawa Finjo survived only because he had returned to his ancestral home for a funeral and was away from Syapru Besi when the flood struck. 
He lost his son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren, while about 40 relatives across both sides of his family are also missing or dead. 
Much of Syapru Besi, a town popular with trekkers and tourists, has been washed away, leaving only a few structures standing on higher ground. 
Finjo says rebuilding the devastated valley could take 15 to 20 years, highlighting the enormous challenge facing communities still recovering from the disaster. 

Al Jazeera's Tony Cheng reports from Rasuwa district, Nepal.

recentItems.title: Trump calls AI safety warnings a 'hoax' as tech leaders raise alarm
recentItems.description:
The US president is brushing aside warnings about the risks of artificial intelligence (AI).
Donald Trump has called them a hoax and a scam.
Some of the biggest names in tech say AI is moving too fast, without enough safeguards in place.
China's top spy chief warned the tech could threaten the ruling Communist Party and rejected calls for the US to block Beijing's AI sector.
Trump says the US can't afford to slow down and risk losing its lead over China.

Al Jazeera’s Manuel Rapalo reports from Washington, DC.
